'''Eske Willerslev''' (born 5 June 1971) is a Danish [[Evolutionary biology|evolutionary geneticist]] notable for his pioneering work in molecular anthropology, palaeontology and ecology. He currently holds the Prince Philip Professorship in Ecology and Evolution at [[University of Cambridge]],<ref name=gs>{{Google scholar id}}</ref><ref name=epmc>{{EuropePMC|0000-0002-7081-6748}}</ref> UK and the Lundbeck Foundation Professorship in Evolution at [[University of Copenhagen|Copenhagen University, Denmark.]] He is director of the [[Centre for Geogenetics|Centre of Excellence in GeoGenetics]], a research associate at the [[Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute]] and a professorial fellow at [[St John's College, Cambridge]].<ref name=zimmer/> Willerslev is a foreign associate of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] (US) and holds the [[Order of the Dannebrog]] issued by her Majesty [[Margrethe II of Denmark|Queen Margrethe II of Denmark]] in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2017-12-12|title=Modtagere af danske dekorationer|url=https://www.kongehuset.dk/modtagere-af-danske-dekorationer|access-date=2021-09-05|website=Kongehuset|language=da|archive-date=18 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210418142224/https://www.kongehuset.dk/modtagere-af-danske-dekorationer}}</ref><ref>Kristian Leth and Eske Willerslev (2016): "''Historien om det hele - fortællinger om magi og videnskab''", People´sPress {{in lang|da}}.<br />Debate book about the concepts of [[Magic (supernatural)|magic]] and [[science]]</ref><ref>Kristoffer Frøkjær (2015): "''Eske Willerslev - Han gør det døde levende''", Gyldendal {{in lang|da}}. Biographic book by [[science journalist]] Kristoffer Frøkjær.</ref><ref>Eske Willerslev (2008): "''Fra pelsjæger til professor - en personlig rejse gennem fortidens dna-mysterier''", Jyllands-Posten {{in lang|da}}.<br />An autobiography.</ref>

==Early life and education==
Willerslev was born in [[Gentofte]], north of Copenhagen, as the son of historian Richard Willerslev and Lona Loell Willerslev. He has a younger sister, Anne Willerslev, an ophthamologist, and an [[identical twin]] brother, [[Rane Willerslev]], an anthropologist and director of the [[National Museum of Denmark]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=2021-08-16 |title=Nærdødsoplevelser - sådan noget, videnskaben har rynket på næsen af • POV International |url=https://pov.international/naerdodsoplevelser/ |access-date=2025-11-11 |work=POV |language=da-DK}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Ny direktør for Nationalmuseet |url=https://natmus.dk/presse-og-nyheder/ny-direktoer-for-nationalmuseet/ |access-date=2025-11-11 |website=Nationalmuseet |language=da}}</ref> He attended Ordrup Gymnasium.<ref>{{Cite web |last=lines |title=Eske Willerslev |url=https://ufm.dk/forskning-og-innovation/forskningsformidling/eliteforsk/prismodtagere/tidligere-prismodtagere/prismodtagere-2011/eske-willerslev |access-date=2025-11-11 |website=Uddannelses- og Forskningsministeriet |language=da}}</ref>

Before becoming a scientist Willerslev led several expeditions in [[Siberia]] in the early 1990s with his twin brother,{{Citation needed|date=November 2025|reason=Source needed for participation of twin brother}} collecting [[Ethnography|ethnographic]] materials and [[megafauna]] skeleton remains. These objects are stored at the Danish [[Moesgaard Museum]], the largest Siberian ethnographical collection in Denmark.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Eske Willerslev |url=https://researchprofiles.ku.dk/en/persons/eske-willerslev/ |access-date=2025-11-11 |website=University of Copenhagen Research Portal |language=en-GB}}</ref> Willerslev also lived as a [[fur trapper]] in the [[Sakha Republic|Sakha (Yakutia) Republic]] from 1993 to 1994.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20120415103151/http://www.science.ku.dk/nyheder/02062008/ Fra pelsjæger til Professor]. science.ku.dk. 2 June 2008</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://politiken.dk/magasinet/interview/ECE2619778/det-begyndte-med-en-droem-om-at-blive-indianer/|title=Det begyndte med en drøm om at blive indianer|date=10 April 2015|work=politiken.dk|access-date=15 December 2016|language=da|archive-date=10 November 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151110093430/http://politiken.dk/magasinet/interview/ECE2619778/det-begyndte-med-en-droem-om-at-blive-indianer/|url-status=live}}</ref> 
He obtained his [[Doctor of Science]] (DSc) degree from Copenhagen University in 2004.<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=DSc|last=Willerslev|first= Eske|year=2004|title= Recovery and analysis of ancient DNA from ice, sediments, and fossil remains|publisher=University of Copenhagen|oclc=474279492}} pp. 1–346, HCØ tryk, University of Copenhagen, Denmark</ref>

==Career==
In 2003 Willerslev moved to the University of Oxford as an independent [[Wellcome Trust]] Fellow, a position he held until 2005.<ref name=":0" /> In 2004, at the age of 33, he became a full professor at [[University of Copenhagen]], making him the youngest professor in Denmark at the time.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Eske Willerslev: The pioneer of environmental DNA {{!}} Villum Fonden |url=https://villumfonden.dk/en/article/eske-willerslev-pioneer-environmental-dna |access-date=2025-11-11 |website=villumfonden.dk |language=en}}</ref> In 2014 he became an adopted member of the Crow Tribe in Montana ([[Crow people|Apsaalooke]]), where he carries the name ChiitdeeXia'ssee (Well Known Scout).<ref name="Crow">{{Cite web| title = For Crow-indianerne er han "Well-known Wolf"| work = www.b.dk| date = 6 July 2014| access-date = 7 October 2014| url = http://www.b.dk/nationalt/for-crow-indianerne-er-han-well-known-wolf| archive-date = 5 December 2014| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20141205172055/http://www.b.dk/nationalt/for-crow-indianerne-er-han-well-known-wolf| url-status = live}}</ref> In 2015 Willerslev took up the Prince Philip Professorship of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at University of Cambridge.<ref name=":0" /> 

Willerslev is a Foreign Associate Member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] (USA),<ref>{{Cite web| title = Eske Willerslev| access-date = 7 October 2014| url = https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/eske-willerslev-4cwuig/| archive-date = 11 October 2014| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20141011163805/http://www.nasonline.org/member-directory/members/20033198.html| url-status = live}}</ref> an elected member of the [[Royal Danish Academy of Sciences and Letters]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=VIDENSKABERNES SELSKAB |access-date=7 October 2014 |url=http://www.royalacademy.dk/Medlemmer.aspx?ID=33&userid=727 |archive-date=12 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141012021915/http://www.royalacademy.dk/Medlemmer.aspx?ID=33&userid=727 |url-status=live}}</ref> and an [[Honorary degree|honorary doctor]] at both [[University of Oslo]] and [[University of Tartu]].<ref name=":0" /> He also holds the [[Order of the Dannebrog]], an [[Order of chivalry|order of chivarly]] issued by Queen Margrethe II of Denmark.<ref>{{Cite web| title = Ancient and environmental DNA studies – Centre for Ecological and Evolutionary Synthesis| access-date = 7 October 2014| url = http://www.mn.uio.no/cees/english/research/news/events/research/others/2014/ancient-and-environmental-dna.html| archive-date = 11 October 2014| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20141011232658/http://www.mn.uio.no/cees/english/research/news/events/research/others/2014/ancient-and-environmental-dna.html| url-status = live}}</ref> He has been a visiting professor at the University of Oxford and a Visiting [[Miller Institute|Miller Professor]] at the University of California, Berkeley.<ref name=":0" />

Willerslev has received several awards including the [[Antiquity (journal)#Prizes|Antiquity Prize]] for the best paper in the journal [[Antiquity (journal)|Antiquity]] in 2009,<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2010 |title=Editorial |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/antiquity/article/editorial/11E28C83DCF5E4538B8B795FE8B6E282 |journal=Antiquity |language=en |volume=84 |issue=324 |pages=293–298 |doi=10.1017/S0003598X00066588 |issn=0003-598X}}</ref> the Danish Independent Research Council's Major [[EliteForsk Prize]],<ref>{{Cite web
| title = Eske Willerslev — EliteForsk | access-date = 7 October 2014 | url = http://eliteforsk.dk/modtagere/prismodtagere-2011/modtagere-af-videnskabsministerens-eliteforsk-priser/eske-willerslev | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20141011183608/http://eliteforsk.dk/modtagere/prismodtagere-2011/modtagere-af-videnskabsministerens-eliteforsk-priser/eske-willerslev
| archive-date = 11 October 2014 }}</ref> the [[DR (broadcaster)#Awards and competitions|Rosenkjær award]] for science communication,<ref>{{Cite web | title = Rosenkjær-foredrag med Eske Willerslev | date = 12 September 2013 | work = dr.dk
| url = http://www.dr.dk/arkivP1/rosenkjaer/Eske_Willerslev/20130912093807.htm | access-date = 7 October 2014 | archive-date = 27 October 2014 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20141027165051/http://www.dr.dk/arkivP1/rosenkjaer/Eske_Willerslev/20130912093807.htm | url-status = live }}</ref> and the Genius Award (Geniusprisen) of Danish Science journalists for "an impressive array of research successes in the public eye, combined with a unique tour-de-force through university".<ref>{{Cite web | last = cawa | title = DNA-forsker Eske Willerslev fik hæderspris | access-date = 7 October 2014 | date = 16 June 2009 | url = http://snm.ku.dk/SNMnyheder/nyheder/290802014/ | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20141011052106/http://snm.ku.dk/SNMnyheder/nyheder/290802014/ | archive-date = 11 October 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | title = Geniusprisen | access-date = 7 October 2014 | quote = Eske Willerslev har en imponerende række af formidlingssucceser i offentligheden bag sig kombineret med en enestående tour-de-force gennem universitetsverdenen [...] Begge har beriget Danmark med formidling af højeste karat og Danske Videnskabsjournalister er stolte af at kunne hædre de to forskere. | url = http://www.videnskabsformidling.dk/geniusprisen/ | archive-date = 12 October 2014 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20141012090322/http://www.videnskabsformidling.dk/geniusprisen/ | url-status = live }}</ref> In 2023 he was awarded the [[List of Balzan Prize recipients|Balzan Prize]].<ref>[https://www.balzan.org/en/prizewinners Balzan Prize 2023]</ref>

==Research==

===Environmental DNA===
During his MSc project Willerslev and colleagues were the first to obtain ancient DNA directly from [[Ice core|ice cores]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Willerslev | first1 = E | last2 = Hansen | first2 = AJ | last3 = Christensen | first3 = B | last4 = Steffensen | first4 = JP | last5 = Arctander | first5 = P | year = 1999 | title = Diversity of Holocene life-forms in fossil glacier ice | journal = Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA | volume = 96 | issue = 14| pages = 8017–8021 | doi=10.1073/pnas.96.14.8017| pmc = 22180 | bibcode = 1999PNAS...96.8017W | pmid=10393940| doi-access = free }}</ref> Later Willerslev and his team expanded on this approach and were the first to show that DNA from plants, mammals, and birds can be obtained directly from ancient as well as modern environmental samples ([[environmental DNA]]).<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Willerslev | first1 = E. | last2 = Hansen | first2 = Anders J. | last3 = Binladen | first3 = Jonas | last4 = Brand | first4 = Tina B. | last5 = Gilbert | first5 = M. Using environmental DNA, Willerslev and collaborators estimated that woolly mammoth in mainland Alaska survived more than 3,500 years earlier than previously thought, thereby dismissing the [[Quaternary extinction event#Mainstream hypotheses|Blitzkrieg and Impact hypotheses]] for megafauna extinction.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1073/pnas.0912510106 |pmid=20018740 |pmc=2795395 |title=Ancient DNA reveals late survival of mammoth and horse in interior Alaska |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=106 |issue=52 |pages=22352–7 |year=2009 |last1=Haile |first1=James |last2=Froese |first2=Duane G |last3=MacPhee |first3=Ross D. Thomas P |last10=Nielsen |first10=Rasmus |last11=Ho |first11=Simon Y. W |last12=Goebel |first12=Ted |last13=Graf |first13=Kelly E |last14=Byers |first14=David |last15=Stenderup |first15=Jesper T |last16=Rasmussen |first16=Morten |last17=Campos |first17=Paula F |last18=Leonard |first18=Jennifer A |last19=Koepfli |first19=Klaus-Peter |last20=Froese |first20=Duane |last21=Zazula |first21=Grant |last22=Stafford |first22=Thomas W |last23=Aaris-Sørensen |first23=Kim |last24=Batra |first24=Persaram |last25=Haywood |first25=Alan M |last26=Singarayer |first26=Joy S|author26-link=Joy Singarayer|last27=Valdes |first27=Paul J |last28=Boeskorov |first28=Gennady |last29=Burns |first29=James A |last30=Davydov |first30=Sergey P |display-authors=29 |bibcode=2011Natur.479..359L }}</ref> and the decline of protein-rich forbs during the Pleistocene extinctions.<ref name=pmid24499916/>

In 2017 Willerslev's team was the first to apply a [[Metagenomics|metagenomic]] approach to environmental DNA, reconstructing the [[Ecological succession|biological succession]] of North America's interior [[Peopling of the Americas|Ice-Free Corridor]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/nature19085 |pmid=27509852 |title=Postglacial viability and colonization in North America's ice-free corridor |journal=Nature |volume=537 |issue=7618 |pages=45–49 |year=2016 |last1=Pedersen |first1=Mikkel W |last2=Ruter |first2=Anthony |last3=Schweger |first3=Charles |last4=Friebe |first4=Harvey |last5=Staff |first5=Richard A |last6=Kjeldsen |first6=Kristian K |last7=Mendoza |first7=Marie L. Z |last8=Beaudoin |first8=Alwynne B |last9=Zutter |first9=Cynthia |last10=Larsen |first10=Nicolaj K |last11=Potter |first11=Ben A |last12=Nielsen |first12=Rasmus |last13=Rainville |first13=Rebecca A |last14=Orlando |first14=Ludovic |last15=Meltzer |first15=David J |last16=Kjær |first16=Kurt H |last17=Willerslev |first17=Eske |bibcode=2016Natur.537...45P |s2cid=4450936 |url=https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:0463dc92-986c-49c7-9ee2-ec85dfe1e62f |access-date=29 August 2020 |archive-date=22 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210722171052/https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:0463dc92-986c-49c7-9ee2-ec85dfe1e62f |url-status=live |doi-access=free }}</ref> Environmental DNA analyses showed the Ice-Free Corridor's transition from being a steppe environment with mammoth and bison, to an open populous-dominated forest inhabited by elk, and ending as the conifer forest with species like moose of today. They also claim the interior Ice-Free Corridor is not the first route for early Americans moving south to lower North America from Alaska, given that it first became viable for human occupation 12.6 thousand years ago, i.e., after [[Clovis culture|Clovis and pre-Clovis]] occupation was seen in the lower 48 states.

Willerslev and his team obtained and identified two-million-year-old environmental DNA sequences from the [[Kap Kobenhavn Formation|Kap København Formation]] in Greenland that indicated that the region once had a forested ecosystem with a wide variety of animal life. They published their results in December 2022.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Callaway | first=Ewen | title=Oldest-ever DNA shows mastodons roamed Greenland 2 million years ago | journal=Nature | volume=612 | issue=7940 | date=2022-12-15 | issn=0028-0836 | doi=10.1038/d41586-022-04377-x | page=384| pmid=36476770 | bibcode=2022Natur.612..384C }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Morelle | first=Rebecca | title=Oldest DNA reveals two-million-year-old lost world | website=BBC Home | date=December 7, 2022 | url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-63867164 | access-date=February 24, 2024}}</ref>

===Ice Age megafaunal extinctions===

Willerslev led the team that published in 2011 a large-scale [[Genetics|genetic study]] on the population dynamics of six Late Pleistocene megafaunal species across the northern hemisphere: woolly mammoth, woolly rhinoceros, horse, reindeer, muskox, and reindeer, coupling their genetic data with climate niche modelling and the [[archaeological record]].<ref name=pmid22048313/> They found that climate has been a major driver of population change over the past 50 thousand years. However, each species responded differently to the effects of climatic change and human contact. Climate change can explain the [[extinction]] the Eurasian musk ox and woolly rhinoceros, while it is more likely that a combination of climate and humans was responsible for the extinction of Eurasian steppe bison and wild horse. The causes behind the extinction of the woolly mammoth were ambiguous.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/news.2011.626 |title=How mammoths lost the extinction lottery |journal=Nature |year=2011 |last1=Callaway |first1=Ewen }}</ref> They did not find any [[Genomic signature|genetic signature]] or any distinctive [[Species distribution|range dynamics]] distinguishing extinct (woolly mammoth and rhino) from surviving species (horse, musk ox, and reindeer), revealing the challenges associated with predicting future responses of extant mammals to climate and human-derived change to their habitats.

===First whole-genome sequencing of an ancient human===
In 2010 a team led by Willerslev [[Sequencing|sequenced]] the genome of a 4,000-year-old man from the [[Saqqaq culture]] of Greenland from his hair. This was the first whole-genome sequencing of an ancient human. The DNA obtained from the hair was fragmented into an average size of 55 [[Base pair|base pairs]].<ref name=pmid20148029>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/nature08835 |pmid=20148029 |title=Ancient human genome sequence of an extinct Palaeo-Eskimo |journal=Nature |volume=463 |issue=7282 |pages=757–62 |year=2010 |last1=Rasmussen |first1=Morten |last2=Li |first2=Yingrui |last3=Lindgreen |first3=Stinus |last4=Pedersen |first4=Jakob Skou |last5=Albrechtsen |first5=Anders |last6=Moltke |first6=Ida |last7=Metspalu |first7=Mait |last8=Metspalu |first8=Ene |last9=Kivisild |first9=Toomas |last10=Gupta |first10=Ramneek |last11=Bertalan |first11=Marcelo |last12=Nielsen |first12=Kasper |last13=Gilbert |first13=M. ===Early peopling of the Americas===
In 2008 Willerslev led the DNA study on [[Coprolite|coprolites]] from the [[Paisley Caves]] in Oregon showing human presence in North America more than 14,000 years ago and about 1000 years prior to [[Clovis Complex|Clovis]].<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1126/science.1154116| pmid = 18388261| title = DNA from Pre-Clovis Human Coprolites in Oregon, North America| journal = Science| volume = 320| issue = 5877| pages = 786–9| year = 2008| last1 = Gilbert | first1 = M. T. P.| last2 = Jenkins | first2 = D. L.| last3 = Gotherstrom | first3 = A.| last4 = Naveran | first4 = N.| last5 = Sanchez | first5 = J. J.| last6 = Hofreiter | first6 = M.| last7 = Thomsen | first7 = P. F.| last8 = Binladen | first8 = J.| last9 = Higham | first9 = T. F. G.| last10 = Yohe | first10 = R. M.| last11 = Parr | first11 = R.| last12 = Cummings | first12 = L. S.| last13 = Willerslev | first13 = E.| bibcode = 2008Sci...320..786G| s2cid = 17671309}}</ref>

In 2013 his team discovered a genetic link between western Eurasians and Native Americans by sequencing the genome of the 24,000-year-old [[Mal'ta-Buret' culture|Mal´ta boy]] from central Siberia, showing that all contemporary Native Americans carry approximately 1/3 of their genome from the Mal'ta population.<ref name=pmid24256729/>

In 2014 his team sequenced the Clovis-age genome from the 12,600-year-old [[Anzick-1|Anzick boy from Montana]] and found it to be ancestral to many contemporary Native Americans, thereby rejecting the [[Solutrean theory]] for early peopling of the Americas.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1038/nature13025| pmid = 24522598| title = The genome of a Late Pleistocene human from a Clovis burial site in western Montana| journal = Nature| volume = 506| issue = 7487| pages = 225–229| date = 2014-02-13| last1 = Rasmussen | first1 = M. | last2 = Anzick | first2 = S. In 2015 Willerslev's team sequenced the genome of the [[Kennewick Man]], a ca. 8,500 year old skeleton whose origin have been heavily debated. The DNA analyses showed Kennewick to be more closely related to Native Americans than to any other contemporary groups and rejecting claims of Kennewick Man being closely related to Japanese [[Ainu people|Ainu]] or Europeans.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Rasmussen | first1 = M | last2 = Sikora | first2 = M | last3 = Albrechtsen | first3 = A | last4 = Korneliussen | first4 = TS | last5 = Moreno-Mayar | first5 = JV | last6 = Poznik | first6 = GD | last7 = Zollikofer | first7 = CPE | last8 = Ponce | last9 = de León | first9 = MS | last10 = Allentoft | first10 = ME | last11 = Moltke | first11 = I | last12 = Jónsson | first12 = H | last13 = Valdiosera | first13 = C | last14 = Malhi | first14 = RS | last15 = Orlando | first15 = L | last16 = Bustamante | first16 = CD | last17 = Stafford Jr | first17 = T | last18 = Meltzer | first18 = DJ | last19 = Nielsen | first19 = R | last20 = Willerslev | first20 = Eske | year = 2015 | title = The ancestry and affiliations of Kennewick Man | journal = Nature | volume = 523| issue = 7561| pages = 455–8| doi = 10.1038/nature14625 | pmid=26087396 | pmc=4878456| bibcode = 2015Natur.523..455R }}</ref>

How the first people migrated from Siberia into the Americas has been a topic of discussion. Two theories dominated: 1) People migrated through an ice-free corridor between the ice masses which covered large areas of North America around the end of the [[Last Glacial Period|last ice age]]. 2) People migrated along the Pacific coast. In a 2016 paper in [[Nature (journal)|Nature]], a [[scientific journal]], Willerslev and co-authors showed that this ice-free corridor could not sustain humans until much later, thereby making it most likely that the early Americans migrated along the Pacific coast.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://geogenetics.ku.dk/latest-news/alle_nyheder/2016/textbook-story-of-how-humans-populated-america-is-biologically-unviable-study-finds/|title=Textbook story of how humans populated America is "biologically unviable", study finds|first=Uffe|last=Wilken|date=10 August 2016|work=ku.dk|access-date=15 December 2016|archive-date=21 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161221042424/http://geogenetics.ku.dk/latest-news/alle_nyheder/2016/textbook-story-of-how-humans-populated-america-is-biologically-unviable-study-finds/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2018 Willerslev's team found a new group of peoples in the Americas that they termed "[[Ancient Beringian|Ancient Beringians]]" – the earliest group of Native Americans to have diversified.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/nature25173 |pmid=29323294 |title=Terminal Pleistocene Alaskan genome reveals first founding population of Native Americans |journal=Nature |volume=553 |issue=7687 |pages=203–207 |year=2018 |last1=Moreno-Mayar |first1=J. Víctor |last2=Potter |first2=Ben A |last3=Vinner |first3=Lasse |last4=Steinrücken |first4=Matthias |last5=Rasmussen |first5=Simon |last6=Terhorst |first6=Jonathan |last7=Kamm |first7=John A |last8=Albrechtsen |first8=Anders |last9=Malaspinas |first9=Anna-Sapfo |last10=Sikora |first10=Martin |last11=Reuther |first11=Joshua D |last12=Irish |first12=Joel D |last13=Malhi |first13=Ripan S |last14=Orlando |first14=Ludovic |last15=Song |first15=Yun S |last16=Nielsen |first16=Rasmus |last17=Meltzer |first17=David J |last18=Willerslev |first18=Eske |bibcode=2018Natur.553..203M |s2cid=4454580 |url=http://researchonline.ljmu.ac.uk/id/eprint/7887/1/UpwardSun_Nature%20paper%20MS%20DEC17.pdf |access-date=4 March 2020 |archive-date=25 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210225051252/http://researchonline.ljmu.ac.uk/id/eprint/7887/1/UpwardSun_Nature |url-status=live }}</ref> This was done through sequencing the genome of an 11.5-thousand-year-old skeleton from Upward Sun River (USR) in Alaska. From this genome they could infer that:
# the initial split between East Asians and Native Americans happened around 36 thousand years ago, with [[gene flow]] persisting until around 25 thousand years ago, likely when this group entered the Americas from Siberia. 
# Gene flow from the Maltá-like ancestor in Siberia into all Native Americans<ref name="pmid24256729" /> took place 25–20 thousand years ago, i.e., just around the time of entrance into the Americas.
# That Ancient Beringians diversified from other Native Americans some 22–18.1 thousand years ago and are thus [[Basal (phylogenetics)|basal]] to the northern and southern Native American branches that diversified around 17.5–14.6-11.5 thousand years and to which all other Native Americans belong. 
# That, after 11.5 thousand years, some of the northern Native American populations received gene flow from a Siberian population more closely related to [[Koryaks]] than to Palaeo-Eskimos, Inuit, or [[Ket people|Kets]] as has previously been suggested. 
# That Native American gene flow into Inuit was through northern and not southern Native American groups as previously argued by the Reich group.

Their findings finally suggest that the far-northern North American presence of northern Native Americans is from a back migration that replaced or absorbed the initial [[Founder effect|founding population]] of "Ancient Beringians".{{citation needed|date=September 2018}}

===Early peopling of Europe===
Willerslev's team sequenced the genome of one of the earliest anatomically modern humans from Europe, [[Kostenki 14]] from Russia, dated to be between 36-38,000 years old.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1126/science.aaa0114 |pmid=25378462 |title=Genomic structure in Europeans dating back at least 36,200 years |journal=Science |volume=346 |issue=6213 |pages=1113–8 |year=2014 |last1=Seguin-Orlando |first1=A |last2=Korneliussen |first2=T. S |last3=Sikora |first3=M |last4=Malaspinas |first4=A.-S |last5=Manica |first5=A |last6=Moltke |first6=I |last7=Albrechtsen |first7=A |last8=Ko |first8=A |last9=Margaryan |first9=A |last10=Moiseyev |first10=V |last11=Goebel |first11=T |last12=Westaway |first12=M |last13=Lambert |first13=D |last14=Khartanovich |first14=V |last15=Wall |first15=J. D |last16=Nigst |first16=P. R |last17=Foley |first17=R. A |last18=Lahr |first18=M. M |last19=Nielsen |first19=R |last20=Orlando |first20=L |last21=Willerslev |first21=E |bibcode=2014Sci...346.1113S |s2cid=206632421 |url=https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/handle/1810/246496 |access-date=29 August 2020 |archive-date=29 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200729043303/https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/handle/1810/246496 |url-status=live }}</ref> The results show that most of the major genetic components present in Europeans today were present in Europe from early on. In 2014 his team undertook the first large scale past population genomic study reporting more than 100 ancient genomes from [[Bronze Age]] Europe and Asia.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/nature14507 |pmid=26062507 |title=Population genomics of Bronze Age Eurasia |journal=Nature |volume=522 |issue=7555 |pages=167–72 |year=2015 |last1=Allentoft |first1=Morten E |last2=Sikora |first2=Martin |last3=Sjögren |first3=Karl-Göran |last4=Rasmussen |first4=Simon |last5=Rasmussen |first5=Morten |last6=Stenderup |first6=Jesper |last7=Damgaard |first7=Peter B |last8=Schroeder |first8=Hannes |last9=Ahlström |first9=Torbjörn |last10=Vinner |first10=Lasse |last11=Malaspinas |first11=Anna-Sapfo |last12=Margaryan |first12=Ashot |last13=Higham |first13=Tom |last14=Chivall |first14=David |last15=Lynnerup |first15=Niels |last16=Harvig |first16=Lise |last17=Baron |first17=Justyna |last18=Casa |first18=Philippe Della |last19=Dąbrowski |first19=Paweł |last20=Duffy |first20=Paul R |last21=Ebel |first21=Alexander V |last22=Epimakhov |first22=Andrey |last23=Frei |first23=Karin |last24=Furmanek |first24=Mirosław |last25=Gralak |first25=Tomasz |last26=Gromov |first26=Andrey |last27=Gronkiewicz |first27=Stanisław |last28=Grupe |first28=Gisela |last29=Hajdu |first29=Tamás |last30=Jarysz |first30=Radosław |display-authors=29 |bibcode=2015Natur.522..167A |s2cid=4399103 |url=https://depot.ceon.pl/handle/123456789/13155 |access-date=29 August 2020 |archive-date=20 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210520091158/https://depot.ceon.pl/handle/123456789/13155 |url-status=live |doi-access=free }}</ref> They found that [[lactose tolerance]], common in northern Europe today, was not common even as late as 2,000 years ago. They also found evidence for major population movements and replacements in both Europe and Asia during the Bronze Age time and that significant parts of contemporary European and Asian genetic diversity were created during this period. They later showed that plague was a likely driver of Bronze Age population dynamics, which as of 2015 is the oldest genomes of ''[[Yersinia pestis]]'' (the [[Etiology|etiological]] agent of plague) reported.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.cell.2015.10.009 |pmid=26496604 |title=Early Divergent Strains of Yersinia pestis in Eurasia 5,000 Years Ago |journal=Cell |volume=163 |issue=3 |pages=571–82 |year=2015 |last1=Rasmussen |first1=Simon |last2=Allentoft |first2=Morten Erik |last3=Nielsen |first3=Kasper |last4=Orlando |first4=Ludovic |last5=Sikora |first5=Martin |last6=Sjögren |first6=Karl-Göran |last7=Pedersen |first7=Anders Gorm |last8=Schubert |first8=Mikkel |last9=Van Dam |first9=Alex |last10=Kapel |first10=Christian Moliin Outzen |last11=Nielsen |first11=Henrik Bjørn |last12=Brunak |first12=Søren |last13=Avetisyan |first13=Pavel |last14=Epimakhov |first14=Andrey |last15=Khalyapin |first15=Mikhail Viktorovich |last16=Gnuni |first16=Artak |last17=Kriiska |first17=Aivar |last18=Lasak |first18=Irena |last19=Metspalu |first19=Mait |last20=Moiseyev |first20=Vyacheslav |last21=Gromov |first21=Andrei |last22=Pokutta |first22=Dalia |last23=Saag |first23=Lehti |last24=Varul |first24=Liivi |last25=Yepiskoposyan |first25=Levon |last26=Sicheritz-Pontén |first26=Thomas |last27=Foley |first27=Robert A |last28=Lahr |first28=Marta Mirazón |last29=Nielsen |first29=Rasmus |last30=Kristiansen |first30=Kristian |display-authors=29 |pmc=4644222 }}</ref>

===Early peopling of Central and South Asia===

In 2018 Willerslev and colleagues published two papers in Nature and [[Science (journal)|Science]] the same day addressing the population history of Central and Southern Asia.<ref name=pmid29743352>{{cite journal |doi=10.1126/science.aar7711 |pmid=29743352 |pmc=6748862 |title=The first horse herders and the impact of early Bronze Age steppe expansions into Asia |journal=Science |volume=360 |issue=6396 |article-number=eaar7711 |year=2018 |last1=De Barros Damgaard |first1=Peter |last2=Martiniano |first2=Rui |last3=Kamm |first3=Jack |last4=Moreno-Mayar |first4=J. Víctor |last5=Kroonen |first5=Guus |last6=Peyrot |first6=Michaël |last7=Barjamovic |first7=Gojko |last8=Rasmussen |first8=Simon |last9=Zacho |first9=Claus |last10=Baimukhanov |first10=Nurbol |last11=Zaibert |first11=Victor |last12=Merz |first12=Victor |last13=Biddanda |first13=Arjun |last14=Merz |first14=Ilja |last15=Loman |first15=Valeriy |last16=Evdokimov |first16=Valeriy |last17=Usmanova |first17=Emma |last18=Hemphill |first18=Brian |last19=Seguin-Orlando |first19=Andaine |last20=Yediay |first20=Fulya Eylem |last21=Ullah |first21=Inam |last22=Sjögren |first22=Karl-Göran |last23=Iversen |first23=Katrine Højholt |last24=Choin |first24=Jeremy |last25=de la Fuente |first25=Constanza |last26=Ilardo |first26=Melissa |last27=Schroeder |first27=Hannes |last28=Moiseyev |first28=Vyacheslav |last29=Gromov |first29=Andrey |last30=Polyakov |first30=Andrei |display-authors=29 }}</ref><ref name=pmid29743675>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/s41586-018-0094-2 |pmid=29743675 |bibcode=2018Natur.557..369D |title=137 ancient human genomes from across the Eurasian steppes |journal=Nature |volume=557 |issue=7705 |pages=369–374 |year=2018 |last1=Damgaard |first1=Peter de Barros |last2=Marchi |first2=Nina |last3=Rasmussen |first3=Simon |last4=Peyrot |first4=Michaël |last5=Renaud |first5=Gabriel |last6=Korneliussen |first6=Thorfinn |last7=Moreno-Mayar |first7=J. Víctor |last8=Pedersen |first8=Mikkel Winther |last9=Goldberg |first9=Amy |last10=Usmanova |first10=Emma |last11=Baimukhanov |first11=Nurbol |last12=Loman |first12=Valeriy |last13=Hedeager |first13=Lotte |last14=Pedersen |first14=Anders Gorm |last15=Nielsen |first15=Kasper |last16=Afanasiev |first16=Gennady |last17=Akmatov |first17=Kunbolot |last18=Aldashev |first18=Almaz |last19=Alpaslan |first19=Ashyk |last20=Baimbetov |first20=Gabit |last21=Bazaliiskii |first21=Vladimir I |last22=Beisenov |first22=Arman |last23=Boldbaatar |first23=Bazartseren |last24=Boldgiv |first24=Bazartseren |last25=Dorzhu |first25=Choduraa |last26=Ellingvag |first26=Sturla |last27=Erdenebaatar |first27=Diimaajav |last28=Dajani |first28=Rana |last29=Dmitriev |first29=Evgeniy |last30=Evdokimov |first30=Valeriy |hdl=1887/3202709 |s2cid=13670282 |display-authors=29 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> The Science paper deals with the spread of the Bronze Age [[Pastoralism|pastoralists]], such as [[Yamnaya culture|Yamnaya]] and the peoples they met in Asia. They could show that descendants of the 24-thousand-year-old Maltá boy from Siberia<ref name=pmid24256729>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/nature12736 |pmid=24256729 |title=Upper Palaeolithic Siberian genome reveals dual ancestry of Native Americans |journal=Nature |volume=505 |issue=7481 |pages=87–91 |year=2013 |last1=Raghavan |first1=Maanasa |last2=Skoglund |first2=Pontus |last3=Graf |first3=Kelly E |last4=Metspalu |first4=Mait |last5=Albrechtsen |first5=Anders |last6=Moltke |first6=Ida |last7=Rasmussen |first7=Simon |last8=Stafford Jr |first8=Thomas W |last9=Orlando |first9=Ludovic |last10=Metspalu |first10=Ene |last11=Karmin |first11=Monika |last12=Tambets |first12=Kristiina |last13=Rootsi |first13=Siiri |last14=Mägi |first14=Reedik |last15=Campos |first15=Paula F |last16=Balanovska |first16=Elena |last17=Balanovsky |first17=Oleg |last18=Khusnutdinova |first18=Elza |last19=Litvinov |first19=Sergey |last20=Osipova |first20=Ludmila P |last21=Fedorova |first21=Sardana A |last22=Voevoda |first22=Mikhail I |last23=Degiorgio |first23=Michael |last24=Sicheritz-Ponten |first24=Thomas |last25=Brunak |first25=Søren |last26=Demeshchenko |first26=Svetlana |last27=Kivisild |first27=Toomas |last28=Villems |first28=Richard |last29=Nielsen |first29=Rasmus |last30=Jakobsson |first30=Mattias |display-authors=29 |bibcode=2014Natur.505...87R |pmc=4105016 }}</ref> survived in Central Asia until at least 5 thousand years ago and were the occupants of [[Botai]] – an archaeological site in Kazakhstan holding the oldest evidence of [[Domestication of the horse|horse domestication]] some 5-6 thousand years ago. They further showed that, in contrast to Europe, early Bronze Age expansion of Yamnaya into Asia had limited genetic and linguistic impact in either Central Asia or in South Asia, contrary to earlier claims by the Reich group from Harvard. The paper thereby challenges the so-called "[[Kurgan hypothesis|Steppe Hypothesis]]" for early spread of the [[Indo-European languages]] that seem to explain the early expansion of Indo-European languages into Europe but not Asia. The latter is argued to have happened by later Bronze groups, such as the [[Sintashta culture|Sintashta]], and reaching all the way to India and Pakistan.

The accompanying Nature paper is based on 137 ancient human genomes of the Eurasian steppe mainly from the time following the Bronze Age.<ref name=pmid29743675/> They find the genetics of the mounted [[Scythians|Scythian]] groups that dominated the Eurasian steppes throughout the Iron Age were highly diverse, consisting of several ethnicities of European and Asian origins despite its highly uniform culture. Later, Scythians [[Genetic admixture|admixed]] and were replaced by steppe nomads from the east coming out of the [[Xiongnu|Xiongnu confederations]] of Mongolia and China, including the westward-expanding [[Huns]] (fourth–fifth century AD). These were later admixed and replaced by expanding East Asian groups including Genghis Khan in the Medieval period. Accordingly, the events transformed the Eurasian steppes from being inhabited by Indo-European speakers of largely West Eurasian ancestry to the mostly Turkic-speaking groups of the present day, who are primarily of East Asian ancestry. According to Willerslev, this was all due to the long-distance traveling enabled by domestication of the horse.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://magazin.spiegel.de/SP/2018/20/157298262/ |title=Invasion aus der Steppe — DER SPIEGEL 2018/20 |access-date=4 June 2018 |archive-date=22 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201222214007/https://magazin.spiegel.de/SP/2018/20/157298262/ |url-status=live }}{{full citation needed|date=September 2018}}</ref>

===Peopling of Southeast Asia===
In 2018 Willerslev lead an international research team sequencing 26 ancient human genome sequences from across Southeast Asia, some dating back 8 thousand years,<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1126/science.aat3628 |pmid=29976827 |bibcode=2018Sci...361...88M |title=The prehistoric peopling of Southeast Asia |journal=Science |volume=361 |issue=6397 |pages=88–92 |year=2018 |last1=McColl |first1=Hugh |last2=Racimo |first2=Fernando |last3=Vinner |first3=Lasse |last4=Demeter |first4=Fabrice |last5=Gakuhari |first5=Takashi |last6=Moreno-Mayar |first6=J. Víctor |last7=Van Driem |first7=George |last8=Gram Wilken |first8=Uffe |last9=Seguin-Orlando |first9=Andaine |last10=de la Fuente Castro |first10=Constanza |last11=Wasef |first11=Sally |last12=Shoocongdej |first12=Rasmi |last13=Souksavatdy |first13=Viengkeo |last14=Sayavongkhamdy |first14=Thongsa |last15=Saidin |first15=Mohd Mokhtar |last16=Allentoft |first16=Morten E |last17=Sato |first17=Takehiro |last18=Malaspinas |first18=Anna-Sapfo |last19=Aghakhanian |first19=Farhang A |last20=Korneliussen |first20=Thorfinn |last21=Prohaska |first21=Ana |last22=Margaryan |first22=Ashot |last23=De Barros Damgaard |first23=Peter |last24=Kaewsutthi |first24=Supannee |last25=Lertrit |first25=Patcharee |last26=Nguyen |first26=Thi Mai Huong |last27=Hung |first27=Hsiao-Chun |last28=Minh Tran |first28=Thi |last29=Nghia Truong |first29=Huu |last30=Nguyen |first30=Giang Hai |display-authors=29 |doi-access=free |hdl=10072/383365 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> 4 thousand years earlier than previous sequences from the region.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.joh.cam.ac.uk/index.php/ancient-dna-testing-solves-100-year-old-controversy-southeast-asian-prehistory |title=Ancient DNA testing solves 100-year-old controversy in Southeast Asian prehistory &#124; StJohns |access-date=9 July 2018 |archive-date=9 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180709154119/https://www.joh.cam.ac.uk/index.php/ancient-dna-testing-solves-100-year-old-controversy-southeast-asian-prehistory |url-status=live }}{{full citation needed|date=September 2018}}</ref> This was made possible by a modified whole genome capture approach. They used this data to test two hypotheses on southeast Asian population history: One theory argues that the indigenous [[Hoabinhian|Hòabìnhian]] hunter-gatherers who populated Southeast Asia from 44,000 years ago adopted agricultural practices independently, without the input from early farmers from East Asia. A second theory, referred to as the 'two-layer model', favours the view that migrating rice farmers from what is now China replaced the indigenous Hòabìnhian hunter-gatherers.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1126/science.aat8662 |pmid=29976814 |bibcode=2018Sci...361...31B |title=The search for ancient DNA heads east |journal=Science |volume=361 |issue=6397 |pages=31–32 |year=2018 |last1=Bellwood |first1=Peter |s2cid=49709899 }}</ref> They determined that neither interpretation fits the complexity of Southeast Asian history and that contemporary Southeast Asians have been influenced by at least four migration waves. The first wave is represented by Hòabìnhian hunter-gatherers who were closely genetically related to traditional hunter-gatherers in Malaysia, the Philippines, and the Andaman Islands (so-called "[[Negrito|negritos]]"). The second wave derived from mainland China and brought with them farming economies such as rice 4000 years ago and mixed with the Hòabìnhians. These were followed by two additional migration waves; by 2 thousand years ago, Southeast Asian individuals carried additional East Asian [[Ancestry-informative marker|ancestry components]]. One component likely represents the introduction of ancestral [[Kra–Dai languages|Kra-Dai languages]] in Mainland southeast Asia, and another the [[Austronesian peoples|Austronesian expansion]] reaching Indonesia 2.1 thousand years ago and the Philippines 1.8 thousand years ago. Among their genomes was also an ancient [[Jōmon people|Jōmon]] genome from Japan that showed shared genetic history with the Hòabìnhians.

===Past disease genetics===

Willerslev's team has been the first to conduct large scale genome sequencing of [[Ancient pathogen genomics|ancient pathogens]]. In 2015 they showed that plague was a likely driver of Bronze Age population dynamics, which as of 2015 represents the oldest reported genomes of ''Yersinia pestis'' (the etiological agent of plague).<ref name="ReferenceA"/> 
Later they showed that westward-expanding Huns carried with them plague that was basal to the [[Plague of Justinian|Justinian plague]], and are thus the likely source of its introduction in Europe killing millions as a result.<ref name=pmid29743352/>
In 2018 they published a large-scale study on ancient genomes of [[Hepatitis B]] (HBV).<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/s41586-018-0097-z |pmid=29743673 |bibcode=2018Natur.557..418M |title=Ancient hepatitis B viruses from the Bronze Age to the Medieval period |journal=Nature |volume=557 |issue=7705 |pages=418–423 |year=2018 |last1=Mühlemann |first1=Barbara |last2=Jones |first2=Terry C |last3=Damgaard |first3=Peter de Barros |last4=Allentoft |first4=Morten E |last5=Shevnina |first5=Irina |last6=Logvin |first6=Andrey |last7=Usmanova |first7=Emma |last8=Panyushkina |first8=Irina P |last9=Boldgiv |first9=Bazartseren |last10=Bazartseren |first10=Tsevel |last11=Tashbaeva |first11=Kadicha |last12=Merz |first12=Victor |last13=Lau |first13=Nina |last14=Smrčka |first14=Václav |last15=Voyakin |first15=Dmitry |last16=Kitov |first16=Egor |last17=Epimakhov |first17=Andrey |last18=Pokutta |first18=Dalia |last19=Vicze |first19=Magdolna |last20=Price |first20=T. Douglas |last21=Moiseyev |first21=Vyacheslav |last22=Hansen |first22=Anders J |last23=Orlando |first23=Ludovic |last24=Rasmussen |first24=Simon |last25=Sikora |first25=Martin |last26=Vinner |first26=Lasse |last27=Osterhaus |first27=Albert D. M. E |last28=Smith |first28=Derek J |last29=Glebe |first29=Dieter |last30=Fouchier |first30=Ron A. M |s2cid=13684815 |display-authors=29 |url=http://urn.kb.se/resolve?urn=urn:nbn:se:su:diva-157746 |access-date=4 March 2020 |archive-date=22 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210722171126/http://su.diva-portal.org/smash/record.jsf?pid=diva2%3A1224162&dswid=-3371 |url-status=live }}</ref> They found evidence of a long-term association of modern HBV genotypes with humans dating back at least 4.5 thousand years, which includes genotypes that are now extinct. They also found that in several cases, the geographical locations of the ancient genotypes do not match present-day distributions. Genotypes that today are typical of Africa and Asia, as well as a subgenotype from India, are shown to have an early Eurasian presence with humans, revealing a complexity of HBV evolution that is not evident when considering modern sequences alone.

Willerslev and collaborators have sequenced the genome of a 700,000-year-old horse from [[Yukon]] in Canada, which as of 2016 was the oldest genome ever sequenced,<ref name=pmid23803765/> until the publication of a million-year-old mammoth genome in 2021.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=van der Valk |first1=T |last2=Pečnerová |first2=P |last3=Díez-Del-Molino |first3=D |last4=Bergström |first4=A |last5=Oppenheimer |first5=J |last6=Hartmann |first6=S |last7=Xenikoudakis |first7=G |last8=Thomas |first8=JA |last9=Dehasque |first9=M |last10=Sağlıcan |first10=E |last11=Fidan |first11=FR |last12=Barnes |first12=I |last13=Liu |first13=S |last14=Somel |first14=M |last15=Heintzman |first15=PD |last16=Nikolskiy |first16=P |last17=Shapiro |first17=B |last18=Skoglund |first18=P |last19=Hofreiter |first19=M |last20=Lister |first20=AM |last21=Götherström |first21=A |last22=Dalén |first22=L |title=Million-year-old DNA sheds light on the genomic history of mammoths. |journal=Nature |date=March 2021 |volume=591 |issue=7849 |pages=265–269 |doi=10.1038/s41586-021-03224-9 |pmid=33597750|pmc=7116897 |bibcode=2021Natur.591..265V }}</ref>

===Outreach===
Willerslev appears regularly in media such as magazines, newspapers, radio and TV when discussions turn to human evolution, migration, and the role of science in society. He and his staff at the [[Centre for Geogenetics|Centre for GeoGenetics]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://geogenetics.ku.dk/|title=GeoGenetics|first=Uffe|last=Wilken|date=7 December 2009|work=ku.dk|access-date=15 December 2016|archive-date=1 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161201235108/http://geogenetics.ku.dk/|url-status=live}}</ref> have participated in documentaries including ''The Great Human Odyssey'' (PBS/CBC/DR)'', Code Breakers'' (CBC/DR) and ''Equus - Story of the Horse'' (CBC/PBS/DR/ZDF), [[First Peoples (TV program)|''First Peoples'' (PBS)]], ''Search for the Head of John the Baptist,'' and ''How to Build and Ancient Man'' (both [[National Geographic]]).{{citation needed|date=September 2018}}
In 2016 he was featured in a profile article in ''[[The New York Times]]''.<ref name=zimmer>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/17/science/eske-willerslev-ancient-dna-scientist.html|title=Eske Willerslev Is Rewriting History With DNA|date=17 May 2016|website=[[The New York Times]]|first=Carl|last=Zimmer|author-link=Carl Zimmer|access-date=15 December 2016|archive-date=18 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161218191752/http://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/17/science/eske-willerslev-ancient-dna-scientist.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Willerslev's work is also featured in the documentary ''Hunt for the Oldest DNA'' which aired on ''[[Nova (American TV program)|Nova]]'' in 2024.<ref>{{citation | last=Anderson | first=John | title='Hunt for the Oldest DNA' Review: Clues of Long-Gone Life | url=https://www.wsj.com/arts-culture/television/hunt-for-the-oldest-dna-review-clues-of-long-gone-life-pbs-nova-919d522f | language=en-US | access-date=February 24, 2024 | page=}}</ref>

==Personal life==
His father's education of Eske and his brother was rather authoritarian and included frequent physical challenges, such as obstacle paths and swimming in ice water, starting from the age of six. His father thought this would help them to become hardy later in life.<ref name="indi" />

Willerslev's father was fiercely [[Atheism|atheist]].<ref name="magi">{{cite web|title=Eske Willerslev: Derfor er videnskab og magi ikke modsætninger (That is why science and magic are not contradictions)|url=https://videnskab.dk/kultur-samfund/eske-willerslev-derfor-er-videnskab-og-magi-ikke-modsaetninger|website=videnskab.dk|date=21 April 2016 |access-date=14 January 2018|language=da|archive-date=16 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180116004253/https://videnskab.dk/kultur-samfund/eske-willerslev-derfor-er-videnskab-og-magi-ikke-modsaetninger|url-status=live}}</ref> However, influenced by numerous experiences living with native people, Willerslev came to respect, and to some extent believe, in supernatural powers unknown to science. Such experiences included encounters with descendants of [[Sitting Bull]] and trapper tribes in Siberia:
<blockquote> "Something similar happened to me when I shot a bear in Siberia. The tradition there is that you pin the bear's head high up in a tree, overlooking where the bear had its hunting grounds. I refused and instead took the bear's head with me home as a trophy. Back home, everything started to go wrong for me and I suffered terrible nightmares. In Siberia the trappers had told me, if I didn't hang up the head as required, all the bears in the world would know about it and hate me for it. I then took a trip to our summer house in Sweden and pinned up the bear's head in a tree there and the nightmares stopped."<ref name="magi" />
</blockquote>
At the age of 32, he was baptized as Christian, although he declares himself as "religious, but not Christian".<ref name="magi" />
Willerslev married Ulrikke Ji Mee Willerslev in 2007. They have two sons, Rasken Willerslev and Bror Willerslev.<ref name="indi">{{cite web|url=http://www.alt.dk/artikler/danmarks-indiana-jones|title=Danmarks Indiana Jones|language=da|website=alt.dk|date=2 May 2016 |access-date=24 April 2017|archive-date=26 April 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170426151246/http://www.alt.dk/artikler/danmarks-indiana-jones|url-status=live}}</ref> The family lives in [[Kongens Lyngby]].
